title: Red Shins, Sore Ankles and Palpitations / Do Not Skip the Heart in Sarcoidosis

blocks.text: Red Shins, Sore Ankles and Palpitations / Do Not Skip the Heart in Sarcoidosis

AMaC MRCP PACES · X-25 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 5) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G · 20 minutes (15 with the patient, then 5 of examiner questions; warning at 13 minutes) · Guidelines: BTS clinical statement on pulmonary sarcoidosis (Thillai et al., Thorax, published online 2 December 2020) · Related AMaC: AMaC Löfgren syndrome station (the same condition without the cardiac trap); this one tests Löfgren syndrome with cardiac involvement

Dear Doctor, a 27-year-old teaching assistant. Three weeks of painful ankles and red lumps on her shins. A chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymph nodes. She wants to know what it is. Please assess and advise.
The patient has consented to see you. Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Red tender shin lumps, ankle arthritis and bilateral hilar nodes in a young woman is Löfgren syndrome, a form of sarcoidosis that often needs no biopsy. Ask about palpitations and do not skip the heart.

The Examiner Trap. She mentions palpitations and a near-faint only if asked. Candidates explain the benign pattern and discharge her on anti-inflammatories. Pass: Löfgren syndrome, ECG, echo, Holter, urgent cardiology review with ECG monitoring. Fail: reassured with no heart check.

rows: Think
Say
Do
Ask about the ankles and shins, then fever, cough, palpitations, fainting, eyes and her calcium or vitamin D tablets.
"Tell me about the ankles and the lumps. Any palpitations or fainting? Any cough, fever, or red eyes?"
Joints; skin; fever; cough; palpitations; syncope; eyes; fatigue; tablets; family history; pregnancy.
Examine the shins, the ankles, the chest and the heart, and look for other skin or eye signs.
"May I look at your shins and ankles and listen to your chest and heart? Tell me if anything hurts."
Shins; ankles; nodes; eyes; skin; pulse; heart sounds; chest; liver; cover her.
Explain what it is, why a biopsy may not be needed, what treats the joints and why the heart is checked.
"This looks like a type of sarcoidosis that often settles by itself. I also want to check your heart rhythm."
Löfgren syndrome; NSAIDs; steroids if needed; ECG; echo; Holter; follow-up; remission.

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are: A 27-year-old teaching assistant. You are fit, anxious and a little tearful.
Opening line: "I've got these red lumps on my shins, and my ankles hurt so much I can hardly walk. Is it serious?"
Volunteered: three weeks. You felt tired and slightly feverish before it started.

Only if asked: your heart sometimes flutters at night. Last week you felt faint on the stairs and had to sit down. No cough. No red eyes. Background, only if asked: no allergies; you do not smoke; you drink a little at weekends; no recent travel; no family history apart from your uncle; you live with two flatmates.
Only if asked about tablets: none; you take the contraceptive pill. You are not pregnant.
Hidden concern (only if asked what worries you): you are afraid of a lung illness like your uncle had. Say: "My uncle died of a lung disease."
Your questions, in your own words: "What is it?" "Will it go away?" "Do I need steroids?"
How you react: if reassured with no heart check, you leave worried. If listened to and offered the tests, you agree. If offered options, you choose.

Findings, released when examined: comfortable; respiratory rate 14; pulse 72 regular; blood pressure 116/68; SpO2 98% on air; temperature 37.4 °C. Tender red nodules on both shins. Both ankles swollen and tender. Chest clear. Heart sounds normal. No lymph nodes, red eyes or skin lesions on the face.

Results, only when requested: blood count, kidney and liver tests normal; calcium normal (recent GP bloods). ECG in clinic: first-degree atrioventricular block. Chest X-ray: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Echo and Holter are requested for after the consultation, so no results are available in the room.

Question ladder: 1. What is the diagnosis? (D, R4) Löfgren syndrome, a form of sarcoidosis. 2. Do you need a biopsy? (D, R4) Not if the picture is typical and nothing points elsewhere. 3. How do you treat the joints? (E, R6) An NSAID; a short tapered steroid course only for significant symptoms. 4. Why check the heart? (E, R6) Palpitations, a near-faint and first-degree AV block may mean cardiac sarcoidosis; arrange echo, Holter, urgent cardiology review with ECG monitoring, and cardiac MRI. 5. How long does it last and how is she followed? (E, R8) Most remit within 2 years; review every 6 months for 2 years.

Curveballs: She asks for steroids at once: reserved for significant symptoms. She faints in clinic: ECG and monitoring, same-day cardiology review. She asks about pregnancy: raise with the specialist team.

Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Pull up your trousers. [R1 Fail] Any cough? [R2 Fail]
CANDIDATE: (Skips the heart.) [R3 Fail] A viral arthritis. [R4 Fail] A biopsy. [R5 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Take ibuprofen and go home; the flutters are anxiety. [R6 Fail] Nothing to worry about. [R7 Fail] Come back in a year. [R8 Fail]

Examiner note: Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): palpitations and near-fainting in sarcoidosis may be heart involvement. No consent, no heart examination, and the diagnosis missed.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I look at your shins and ankles and listen to your chest and heart? Tell me if anything hurts. I'll cover you afterwards. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Any palpitations or fainting? Any cough, fever or red eyes? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: My heart flutters at night, and I felt faint last week.
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) Tender red shin nodules, swollen tender ankles, a clear chest and normal heart sounds. [R3 Pass]
CANDIDATE: This looks like Löfgren syndrome, a form of sarcoidosis; it often needs no biopsy. [R4 Pass]
CANDIDATE: I'd like blood tests, calcium and an ECG today, and a CT only if the picture is atypical. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: An anti-inflammatory for the joints; steroids only if it's severe. I'd also arrange an echo and a Holter because of the flutters. The ECG shows a delay in the heart's conduction, which with your faint turn could mean sarcoid in the heart, so I'll ask the cardiologists for an urgent review with ECG monitoring, and the same day if you faint or the block worsens, and arrange the heart tests quickly. If you feel faint again or your heart races before then, call 999. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: What worries you most? [R7 Pass]
PATIENT: A lung illness, like my uncle.

CANDIDATE: That is fair; most people recover within two years. [R7 Pass] I'll book the heart tests and ask cardiology for an urgent review, with routine follow-up every six months. Is that plan all right with you? [R8 Pass]
Examiner note: Gave the diagnosis, the joint treatment and the heart tests. Did not name other causes, cardiac MRI, steroid doses or a written plan.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: I'm the registrar. May I examine you? Would you like a chaperone? I'll ask about pregnancy only with your permission. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Are you more breathless than your X-ray would explain? Any family history? [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: (Examines.) No lymph nodes, red eyes or facial skin lesions. [R3 High]

CANDIDATE: Tuberculosis, lymphoma and infection are other causes, and erythema nodosum can follow streptococcal infection, the contraceptive pill or bowel disease, but the pattern fits Löfgren syndrome. [R4 High]
CANDIDATE: A CT only if the picture isn't typical. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: If the tests are abnormal, a cardiac MRI or PET and a specialist cardiac team. [R6 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll write to your school if you'd like. [R7 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll give you a written plan and a six-monthly review for two years. [R8 High]
Examiner note: Added a chaperone, other causes, the CT rule, cardiac MRI or PET, a letter for her school and a written plan.
R2: Not asking about palpitations and fainting. They point to heart involvement.
R4: Calling it viral arthritis. Shin nodules, ankle arthritis and hilar nodes together are Löfgren syndrome.
R5: Asking only for a biopsy. A tissue diagnosis can be skipped in typical Löfgren syndrome.

R6: Discharging with palpitations and a near-faint. An ECG and heart tests are needed, and a conduction abnormality with a near-faint needs urgent cardiology review with ECG monitoring, not a routine referral; same day if there is syncope or a higher-degree block.
"Can I ask about your heart? Any palpitations or fainting?"
"Shin nodules, ankle arthritis and hilar nodes fit Löfgren syndrome."
"I'd like to check I've understood what worries you most."

BTS statement (published online 2 December 2020): bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with erythema nodosum or ankle arthritis can often be diagnosed without biopsy if no alternative diagnosis is apparent. Some patients need only NSAIDs; steroids are for significant systemic symptoms, typically 30 to 40 mg daily for 1 to 2 weeks then tapered, usually under 3 months. Most remit within 2 years.

Baseline tests: full blood count, urea and electrolytes, liver tests, calcium, and a 12-lead ECG; CT may be left out if the picture is typical, with a repeat chest X-ray within 3 months and CT if circumstances change. Consider cardiac involvement when breathlessness is disproportionate, or with ECG abnormalities or cardiac symptoms such as a near-faint; ECG and echo, then cardiac MRI or PET if abnormal; offer a 24-hour Holter for palpitations; refer to a specialist cardiac sarcoidosis team. The statement gives no time frame, so urgency is clinical judgement: conduction disease may mean cardiac sarcoidosis, so a near-faint with a conduction abnormality warrants urgent cardiology review with ECG monitoring: same day if there is syncope or a higher-degree block, with admission if symptoms are current, the ECG worsens or there is instability.
Follow-up for Löfgren syndrome: every 6 months for 2 years, then discharge.
THINK: Shins, ankles, hilar nodes: Löfgren; palpitations: check the heart.
SAY: "This often settles; I also want to check your heart."
DO: Ask about palpitations; listen to the heart; ECG.
NUMBERS: Most remit within 2 years; review 6-monthly for 2 years (BTS).
TRAP: Reassured, no heart check.
FINISH: NSAID, ECG, urgent cardiology review with ECG monitoring, echo, Holter, six-monthly review.

Thillai M et al. BTS clinical statement on pulmonary sarcoidosis. Thorax, published online 2 December 2020. https://brit-thoracic.org.uk/document-library/clinical-statements/sarcoidosis/bts-sarcoidosis-clinical-statement Supports: Löfgren syndrome diagnosis and treatment, baseline tests, cardiac sarcoidosis (ECG and echo, 24-hour Holter for palpitations, cardiac MRI or PET to confirm, specialist team; no urgency time frame given) and follow-up.
